Executive Summary The Legacy Device Challenge Legacy devices across grid, transportation, and building systems present complex modernization challenges that extend far beyond simple equipment obsolescence. Pulling from presentations and break-out group discussions from this workshop on legacy devices across all three sectors, this report examines the interconnected factors driving replacement decisions, documents successful modernization initiatives from recent years, and provides strategic guidance for coordinating infrastructure transformation across these critical sectors. Legacy devices, defined herein as existing equipment superseded by newer technologies but still operational, face mounting challenges related to maintenance, integration, and security. While they may function adequately in isola- tion, they increasingly constrain system-wide capabilities. A 1970s transformer reliably converts voltage but lacks monitoring features for managing distributed energy resources. Building controls from the 1990s cannot participate in demand response programs. Transportation sensors designed for traditional traffic cannot support connected vehi- cle applications. Replacement patterns vary substantially across sectors. Grid infrastructure may operate 40-50 years before encountering critical limitations, while transportation and building systems experience more rapid degra- dation (5-15 years) due to environmental exposure. Understanding these lifecycle patterns enables more effective infrastructure modernization planning and resource allocation. Key Replacement Drivers Five primary factors drive legacy device replacement decisions: • Supply Chain Constraints: Legacy devices depend on obsolete components, discontinued manufacturing processes, and sufficient knowledge transfer to new members of the workforce. Replacement parts may re- quire months to procure or custom fabrication. As equipment ages and manufacturers exit markets, supply vulnerabilities intensify, eventually forcing replacement even when devices remain functional. • Physical and Performance Degradation: Equipment degrades through weather exposure, insufficient main- tenance, wear and tear (especially batteries), and technical deprecation (obsolete protocols, discontinued software). Degradation rates vary dramatically by sector and application. • Enhanced Features: Modern devices offer capabilities legacy equipment cannot provide—real-time mon- itoring, dynamic control, system integration, and security features. While some equipment accepts retrofits (thermostats, sensors), others resist modification (commercial HVAC, electrical infrastructure). Compatibility requirements and evolving standards complicate integration. • Funding Cycles: Financial constraints fundamentally shape replacement timing. Public organizations rely on grants with limited availability, causing deferred maintenance and phased upgrades. Some lower-income households may replace equipment more slowly to save up for a high-quality replacement.
